book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction frames The Hobbit as Plato's Allegory of the Cave retold 'there and back again': like the freed prisoner, Bilbo leaves his comfortable hole, has his eyes opened by a frightening journey, and returns 'queer' to neighbors who cannot accept that life offers more than order and routine. It lists the book's guiding questions - whether adventures are worth missing dinner, whether food and song outrank gold, whether powerful technology can be trusted or must be destroyed, and the duties of friends - as the essays' shared agenda.

Bassham reads The Hobbit as a story of moral growth: the comfort-loving Bilbo who trembles like jelly at the dwarves' plans grows into the hobbit who volunteers to carry the Ring to Mordor. Growth in wisdom comes from Socratic self-examination (learning how little one knows) and from broadened experience of the wide world; growth in virtue comes either from sudden conversion (Thorin's Scrooge-like deathbed repentance) or, as Aristotle taught, from slow habituation - Bilbo's repeated courageous and generous acts (sparing Gollum, returning the elf-keys, giving up the Arkenstone) build lasting character. Seneca's view that hardship strengthens supplies the framework for why Bilbo's trials on the road ennobled rather than broke him.

Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.

Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.

Knepp maps Appiah's cosmopolitanism onto Bilbo's journey from provincial hobbit - the Shire-folk who find even across-Brandywine hobbits odd - to citizen of the world who wants the good of dwarves, elves and men. Shared adventure, not argument, teaches tolerance: Bilbo and the dwarves never convert each other but learn to live together through meals, bickering and shared survival, exactly Appiah's 'conversation' that helps people get used to one another. The elf-made swords and the mithril coat show 'cultural contamination' as a good; Gimli and Legolas illustrate fallibilism and pluralism; Smaug and the orcs are anti-cosmopolites who impose their single way by force.

The chapter sets the bloody classical ideal of glory (Homer's kleos, Beowulf, Alexander modeling himself on Achilles) - which Augustine already condemned as libido dominandi - against Plato's alternative of a life aimed at the good, the true and the beautiful. Thorin's last charge at the Battle of Five Armies fits the heroic tradition, but Tolkien's real point is that Bilbo, the 'grocer' who feels the dwarves' treasure-lust yet walks away from it, and who ends by inviting the dwarves to four-o'clock tea instead of a victory feast, shows glory subordinated to domestic beauty and humility. Socrates' question in the Apology - why care so little for wisdom and the soul's improvement while chasing wealth, honor and reputation - is exactly the temptation Bilbo resists, and the Symposium's move from battle to a drinking-party of love-of-beauty mirrors Tolkien's placement of heroism in hobbits rather than warriors.

Garcia argues Tolkien writes with a virtue-ethical moral theory: Middle-earth peoples are characterized by moral traits (noble eagles, cruel orcs), intentions matter (Bilbo is not to blame for the discomforting barrel escape because he meant rescue, and he turns back through the mountain tunnels because loyalty and courage demand it), and the book's drama is the tension between Aristotle's 'great-souled' proper pride and Aquinas' Christian humility. Thorin's pride (self-styled 'King under the Mountain', refusing Bard's just claim), Smaug's vanity that Bilbo flatters to find the bare patch, and the dragon-sickness illustrate pride as vice, while Bilbo's growth - believing after the spiders that 'there was more in him' yet accepting Gandalf's 'you are only quite a little fellow in a wide world' with a laugh - exemplifies correct self-assessment between vanity and undue humility.

The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.

Johnson tests the Battle of Five Armies against just war theory as developed from Augustine through Aquinas: the men under Bard satisfy legitimate authority, just cause and last resort (they bargained, even using the Arkenstone as leverage and trying economic pressure), the Elvenking explicitly waits rather than start 'this war for gold', while the dwarves fail the criteria because greed and pride are not just causes and a thirteenth-share was a cheap price for peace. The war that actually happens - the three armies uniting against Bolg's orc-host - is justified self- and other-defense, whereas the orcs' motives (revenge, plunder, conquest) are unjust. Against apparent pacifist evidence (Tom Bombadil, Frodo at the Shire 'scouring', Gandalf's 'pity' for Gollum), Johnson reads Tolkien's letters as endorsing war as sometimes necessary and sometimes 'in the right', though Tolkien rejects the theory's reasonable-chance-of-success condition given the hopeless stands at Helm's Deep and the Morannon.

Tallon reads The Hobbit as an exercise in aesthetics: Tolkien half-accepts the Kant-era 'art for art's sake' settlement - dwarves once made 'things of beauty for pure delight', elves sing 'lovely nonsense' without shame, Gandalf blows smoke-rings and fireworks - while rejecting both Victorian moralism and Wilde's amoralism. Instead aesthetic sensitivity is a moral thermometer grounded in Augustine's ordo amoris: orcs 'make no beautiful things, but many clever ones', dragons cannot tell good work from bad nor mend a loose scale (which is how Bard's arrow finds Smaug's bare patch), and Aule creates dwarves out of love so others might enjoy the beauty of Ea while Saruman's 'mind of metal and wheels' breeds Uruk-hai for domination. Beauty also acts morally: the dwarves' song awakens Bilbo's 'love of beautiful things made by hands' and, as Scarry and Murdoch hold, that awakening of desire beyond oneself is what prepares us for justice.

O'Hara argues that play is what makes hobbits - and us - fully human: Bilbo's childhood games of throwing stones, riddles and smoke-rings turn out to be training for the quest (his stone-throwing fells the spiders, his riddle-practice buys time with Gollum), and even Gollum's riddle-game makes him momentarily 'less a monster and more a person'. Following Schiller's and Huizinga's Homo ludens thesis that play completes humanity, he distinguishes play from idleness (Aquinas held recreation continues in heaven; Peirce called play 'vigorous exercise'), places leisure among the goods of Aristotle's 'we play in order to be serious', and contrasts Gandalf's beauty-directed fireworks with the orcs' merely useful explosions and work-chants. But play has limits: Kant warns against treating persons as toys, and Bilbo's lesson is 'Never laugh at live dragons!'

Stewart argues Middle-earth magic is rule-bound engineering rather than Hume's miracle as 'a violation of the laws of nature': spells fail, the Ring hides neither shadow nor wet footprints, and magic comes in strengths like gravity, so fear of Gandalf is fear of superior knowledge of nature's laws, not of lawlessness. The deeper point is Tolkien's linkage of magic with technology as the impatient will to make one's will effective quickly - Sauron is 'Lord of magic and machines', the Ring is the supreme technological artifact, Saruman's forged men and blast-fires embody domination - while elvish 'Art' is sub-creation and Beorn's communion with animals models harmony with nature. Like Thoreau pricing possessions in 'how much life' they cost, the chapter ends with Tolkien's warning that 'if a thing can be done, it should be done' is the great false assumption of our age.

Kind uses our genuine reactions to Bilbo - pity when he sits forlorn at the Lonely Mountain, anxiety at the riddle-game, outrage at Thorin's rebuke - to stage the paradox of fiction: how can emotions be rational toward someone we know never existed? She walks through the failed solutions: Radford's verdict that fiction-emotions are irrational like fearing a mountain lion after the sighting is debunked; Walton's 'quasi-emotions' of make-believe, which cannot explain why we cannot switch our fear of the wargs off at will; and thought theory's mental images, since what we fear is Smaug, not our mental image of Smaug. Her preferred route, following Richard Moran, relaxes the belief requirement itself - as Hume noted passions resist rational assessment and as Nussbaum argues fiction cultivates moral character, many emotions (grief for the dead Tolkien, fear of future floods) need no existence beliefs.

Grimwood turns the riddle contest in the dark into a lesson in hermeneutics: Bilbo interprets like Hirsch's intentionalist, asking what Gollum means (and suspecting he means to eat him), while Gollum answers each of Bilbo's riddles by fusing the words with his own forgotten past - sun on daisies, eggs at his grandmother's hole - exactly Gadamer's claim that understanding is a dialogue of horizons shaped by 'prejudices'. Bilbo's final 'What have I got in my pocket?' breaks the game because it severs the good will that makes interpretation a genuine exchange, leaving Gollum no horizon to fuse with, so he simply constructs his own 'truth' that the hobbit stole his precious. The chapter generalizes: Gandalf's dismantling of 'Good morning' shows interpretation is everywhere, and there is no view from nowhere outside our horizons.

Jensen dissects Bilbo's run of luck - the fish that leaps to his feet mid-riddle, the drunken elf-guards, above all his hand falling on the Ring in the dark - using Aristotle's account of luck as the rare, uncontrolled coincidence of ordinary causes (an orc leaving the back door ajar plus a hobbit's six-meals-a-day girth). He then deploys Nagel's kinds of moral luck: Bilbo's constitutive luck (born a Baggins with Took blood, Rawls' 'natural lottery'), circumstantial luck, and resultant luck (finding the Ring, which he could not control but which dooms Sauron). Against Kant's good will that is 'like a jewel' beyond luck and Plato's 'no harm can befall a good man', the chapter argues that Thorin's dragon-sickness, the orcs' unlucky birth, and Bilbo's outcome-dependent standing show that praise and blame do - and should - reach beyond the agent's control.

Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.

Watson uses the company's decisions under uncertainty - whether to approach the troll-fire that nearly gets them eaten, the elf-lights in Mirkwood, Bilbo's descent of Smaug's tunnel - to teach decision theory: expected utility (assigning probabilities and values shows they should have stayed put rather than follow the troll-light), conditional probability (the Mirkwood lights are treated as dependent events, dodging the gambler's fallacy), and simplifying the outcome set. He then judges Bilbo by Aristotle's doctrine that courage is the mean between the vice of cowardice and the vice of rashness, felt with respect to the appropriate passion, fear: Bilbo fears as he should (kettle-whistles and jelly-trembles), avoids unforced risks, yet risks death for his companions' lives - so he has acted courageously and is developing, not yet fully possessing, the virtue, which Aristotle says requires long practice.

Kraus argues The Hobbit is two different books depending on the reader's experience: read cold it is a fairy-tale of adventure, but reread after The Lord of the Rings - knowing what the Ring did to Bilbo and what 'precious' means - it becomes a song of innocence and experience like Blake's Songs and Wordsworth's 'emotion recollected in tranquillity', where Elrond's opening description points to the deep Silmarillion history a first-time reader cannot yet feel. Emerson's 'transparent eye-ball' from Nature - the self stripped bare and made original in the woods - becomes Bilbo's first use of the Ring, where invisibility lets him see Gollum's miserable humanity and choose pity; but the image darkens into Sauron's Lidless Eye, the totalizing knowledge that defines and devours selves. 'There and back again' thus echoes nostos turned nostalgia: Bilbo never truly gets back, having traded the child's innocence Thorin praises on his deathbed for an experience he cannot undo.

holes.name: Sub-creation (Tolkien's theory of art)
holes.what: Tolkien's view (in 'On Fairy-stories') that human artistic making is a subordinate imitation of divine creation, fashioning a Secondary World rather than seeking power over the primary one.
holes.why: Chapters 25 and 27 build their aesthetics on Tolkien's sub-creation - Aule making dwarves so others might enjoy the beauty of Ea, elvish magic as 'Art, not Power' - and no existing taxonomy concept covers it.

holes.name: The Philosophy of Play (Homo Ludens)
holes.what: The tradition (Schiller's play-drive, Huizinga's Homo ludens) holding that free play is constitutive of full humanity and the root of art, ritual and philosophy.
holes.why: Chapter 27 ('Hobbitus Ludens') is organized entirely around play and leisure as what completes humanity, and the taxonomy has no concept for play or leisure.

holes.name: Friedrich Schiller
holes.what: German idealist poet-philosopher whose Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man make the play-drive (Spieltrieb) what reconciles our natures and completes humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 27 quotes Schiller's play thesis ('man is only fully human when he plays') three times as its central philosophical framework.

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of how we can have genuine, rational emotions (fear, pity) toward characters and events we know to be fictional.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is entirely structured around this named paradox as applied to pitying Bilbo and fearing Smaug, and the taxonomy has no concept for it.
